title: Database Upgrades and Compatibility
learning_outcomes: Describe the main purpose and behavior of database upgrades and compatibility.
Apply a small SQLite example involving application upgrades and verify the result.
Identify one failure mode, compatibility constraint, or data-integrity concern related to this topic.

content.intro: This lesson covers database upgrades and compatibility as part of SQLite’s embedded relational database model. Work through one small example, verify the output, and then connect the result to the listed subtopics from the supplied curriculum.
content.why_it_matters: A transaction prevents partial persistence of a related multi-step operation.
content.task: Create a second example for database upgrades and compatibility. Use at least one of these subtopics: Application upgrades, SQLite runtime compatibility, Version-gated features. Predict the result, run it in a local SQLite environment or supported language binding, and document one boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: Include a minimal reproducible SQL statement or application snippet.
State the expected result before execution and compare it to the observed result.
Document one boundary/error case and the SQLite runtime assumptions.
hints: Start from the smallest subtopic and a fixture with only a few known rows.
Write the expected output before running the example; then change one input or predicate and compare.
If a feature fails, verify the linked SQLite version/build and isolate the failing statement before changing the schema.

common_mistakes.why: SQLite has specific type-affinity, NULL, configuration and version behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Check SQLite’s official documentation and the actual linked runtime; reduce to a small fixture.

common_mistakes.why: A query can run successfully while returning incorrect rows or an inflated aggregate.
common_mistakes.fix: Compare output to a hand-calculated expected result and test an edge case.

common_mistakes.why: Destructive SQL and migration experiments can permanently change a database.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a disposable file or in-memory database and verify backups before destructive operations.

summary: Group related writes in one transaction and roll back if any required step fails.
Record SELECT sqlite_version() and the relevant feature/build assumptions.
Keep a reproducible example and expected output so later changes can be regression-tested.
content.run_instructions: Save the SQL to `lesson.sql`; run `sqlite3 -batch practice.db < lesson.sql`. For simple tabular output, add `.headers off` and `.mode list` in the shell or compare the returned rows in your API. Work only in a disposable practice database. content.troubleshooting: Check that the intended database file is open, statement terminators are present, the SQLite version supports the feature, and foreign-key settings are applied on the same connection. Run one statement at a time to isolate errors.
content.reset_steps: Close the shell and delete only the disposable `practice.db` file, or use a fresh `:memory:` connection. Never reset a production database.

items.title: Application upgrades
items.text: Document the preconditions, the expected result, one failure path and the version/build assumptions; verify the behavior with the target runtime rather than inferring success from syntax alone.

items.title: SQLite runtime compatibility
items.text: SQLite has no dedicated DATE/TIME storage class. Choose a consistent ISO-8601 text or integer-epoch convention, document timezone handling, and use date/time functions with understood input formats.

items.title: Version-gated features
items.text: Document the preconditions, the expected result, one failure path and the version/build assumptions; verify the behavior with the target runtime rather than inferring success from syntax alone.

items.title: Testing older database files
items.text: Make tests deterministic with seeded fixtures, documented runtime versions and repeatable commands. Test invalid data, errors, migration/recovery paths and result equivalence; time measurements alone do not prove correctness.

items.title: Supporting rollback and recovery plans
items.text: Put related changes in one explicit transaction and commit only after all required checks succeed. Roll back on failure; a SAVEPOINT provides a rollback point within a transaction rather than a separate independent transaction.

content_blocks.title: Version and runtime note
content_blocks.text: Record `SELECT sqlite_version();` and confirm the SQLite library linked to your application. The shell executable and application binding can use different library versions. Optional extensions and compile-time features may be absent.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself

acceptance_criteria: A minimal reproducible SQL statement or application snippet is included.
The expected result is stated before execution.
The observed result and one boundary/error case are documented.

items.title: Assuming generic SQL behavior
items.text: Check SQLite’s own documentation and the actual linked runtime; standards-compliant engines can still differ in type handling, SQL extensions, and configuration.

items.title: Skipping verification
items.text: Reduce the example to the smallest fixture, inspect the schema and result rows, and repeat after changing one thing at a time.

items.title: Testing on valuable data
items.text: Use a disposable file or an in-memory database and a verified backup before destructive operations.

content_blocks.text: Recap. Group related writes in one transaction and roll back if any required step fails. Keep the database upgrades and compatibility behavior explicit in code and document assumptions that a future maintainer would otherwise have to guess.

accessibility_notes: Use text labels and expected-output text rather than relying on diagram colors alone. SQL output is provided as text; enlarge type or use a screen reader as needed.
version_notes: SQLite feature availability varies with the library version and compile-time options. Verify SELECT sqlite_version() and the application binding before relying on newer features.
